title: Cu oxide/ZnO-based surfaces for a selective ethylene production from gas-phase CO2 electroconversion
abstract: In this work, the application of Cu oxides/ZnO-based electrocatalytic surfaces for the continuous and selective gas-phase electroreduction of CO2 to ethylene in a filter-press type electrochemical cell is studied. The prepared catalytic materials are characterized by transmission electron microscopy, X-ray diffraction and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy. Then, the Cu oxides/ZnO-based gas diffusion electrodes are electrochemically characterized by cyclic voltammetry and Tafel plot analyses. The ethylene formation rate and Faradaic efficiency are as high as 487.9 μmolms and 91.1% when a current density of 7.5 mAcm (-2.5 V vs. Ag/AgCl) is applied to the system, with an ethylene/methane production ratio of 139, showing a better performance than previous electrocatalytic systems for the production of ethylene from CO2 conversion. Consequently, the use of Cu oxides/ ZnO-based electrocatalysts for gas-phase CO2 reduction is a step forward in the production of C2 products, such as ethylene.

In this work, the application of Cu oxides/ZnO-based electrocatalytic surfaces for the continuous and selective gas-phase electroreduction of CO2 to ethylene in a filter-press type electrochemical cell is studied. The prepared catalytic materials are characterized by transmission electron microscopy, X-ray diffraction and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy. Consequently, the use of Cu oxides/ ZnO-based electrocatalysts for gas-phase CO2 reduction is a step forward in the production of C2 products, such as ethylene.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
The reduction of carbon dioxide (CO2) concentration in the atmosphere represents one of the worldwide challenges for the last and next decades due to the several negative effects related to global warming [1]. Among the different methods to mitigate CO2 emissions from the use of fossil fuels, the electrochemical conversion of CO2 into valueadded products is being considered a promising technique to reduce the reliance on fossil fuels helping also to close the carbon cycle adding a new sink [2,3]. Besides, this technology provides a new approach to store energy, otherwise wasted, from intermittent renewable energy sources such as solar or wind energies [4]. Different products such as carbon monoxide (CO), formic acid (HCCOH), alcohols and hydrocarbons can be obtained from CO2 as a function of the number of electrons exchanged and the catalytic material used or applied voltage, among others [5], as shown in Table 1. However, the outstanding stability of the CO2 molecule, which involves high energy requirements, makes the electrochemical transformation of CO2 challenging [6]. In this regard, both the high reaction overpotential and the low selectivity of the process due to the competitive hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) need to be further considered to make this process feasible at industrial scale. Therefore, the development of highly active, cheap, durable, energy efficient and selective electrocatalysts is required to overcome these limitations [7].
Focusing on the production of chemical feedstock and energy-dense fuels such as hydrocarbons (e.g. methane (CH4) and ethylene (C2H4)) due to their interesting applications as energy vectors and chemical building blocks [8,9], different research works have demonstrated that copper (Cu) is the unique material able to electroreduce CO2 with moderate rates, selectivities and Faradaic efficiencies (FEs) [5,10–12]. Nevertheless, the reported yields so far as well as the large required reaction overpotentials are not sufficient for bringing this process closer to commercial applications [7]. As a consequence, two different trends, among others, have been followed in the literature. On the one hand, the development of Cu oxide-based electrocatalysts has attracted the interest of several authors due to their ability to enhance the catalytic activity and the reaction selectivity toward C2 products such as C2H4 [13]. For instance, Ren et al. [14] investigated the selective electrochemical reduction of CO2 to C2H4 and C2H5OH on Cu(I) oxide films. The best selectivity for C2H4 and C2H5OH was achieved at −1.19 V vs. Ag/AgCl using 1.7–3.6 μm thick films with FEs of 34–39 % and 9–16 %, respectively, whereas CH4 formation was suppressed (FE < 1%). In addition, a high C2H4/CH4 ratio up to 100 was obtained. The authors suggested that an optimized density of edges is crucial for the formation of C2 products. Two years later, Wang et al. [15] studied the use of monodispersed Cu oxide nanoparticles (CuOx NP) ensembles for an enhanced C2H4 yield by varying the nanoparticle density. was shown, which involved a decrease in the mean interparticle distance and an increase in the total surface active sites. The authors attributed these findings to dynamically favored conditions for CO readsorption and *CO dimerization. Recently, Yang et al. [9] studied the influence of different supports when using CuO electrocatalysts for the production of C2H4 from CO2 reduction. The use of N-doped carbon (NxC) as support allowed to achieve a higher FE to C2H4 (36%) than those obtained when using a XC-72 carbon black support (19%) and unsupported CuO catalysts (20%), which they related to an increase in the coverage of the CO intermediate when using the NxC support due to a high CO2 concentration near the electrocatalysts that might favor the formation of C2H4 from the coupling of two CO units.
On the other hand, the combination of different metals with Cubased structures is also appealing since this allows tuning the adsorption properties and the binding energies of reaction intermediates for an enhanced reaction selectivity [16], even though further research is still required to better understand the influence of material structure including morphology, size, roughness, etc. [17]. For example, Chang et al. [18] developed Ag-Cu core-shell nanoparticles in an attempt to evaluate the influence of the surface atomic ratios of Ag and Cu. Interesting FEs for CH4 and C2H4 (18% and 25%, respectively) were achieved at −1.26 V vs. Ag/AgCl when the atomic ratio between Ag and Cu was 1:7.63. The authors associated the better activity toward C2H4 under such conditions with an enhancement of *CO adsorption onto the Cu surface. Furthermore, Ma et al. [19] prepared bimetallic Cu-Pd electrocatalysts for the conversion of CO2 into hydrocarbons. The use of a phase-separated structure led to higher selectivities for C2 products (i.e. C2H4 and C2H5OH) with a total FE for these products of 68% at −0.95 V vs. Ag/AgCl, which the authors associated with the neighboring feature of Cu atoms. In this regard, the adsorbed CO is dimerized to the COCOH intermediate that is then converted to C2 products. The ordered materials favored, however, the conversion of CO2 to CH4 due to the presence of Cu-Pd intermetallic structures, which tends to form the CHO intermediate from the adsorbed CO. Recently, Billy and Co [20] developed a bimetallic electrocatalyst based on Ru coated Cu nanoparticles for the electroreduction of CO2 toward a wide range of products. The authors showed the possibility of both tuning the reaction selectivity (CO2 conversion activity was enhanced over the HER) and reducing the onset potential for several CO2 electroreduction species such as C2H4, C2H6 and HCOO−) compared to the use of Cu nanoparticles. These findings were attributed to the improved binding energies of intermediate species, thus demonstrating how the combination of materials can alter the CO2 electroreduction selectivity.
Moreover, previous results in our group showed the importance of particle size for CO2 electroconversion processes. Thus, pure Cu nanoparticles of 60–80 nm were able to continuously electroreduce CO2 in gas phase to CH4 and CO (with H2 as subproduct) in a wide range of applied potentials (i.e.−2.4 to −1.8 V vs. Ag/AgCl) and catalytic loadings (i.e. 0.25 to 1.5 mgcm−2). The best results in terms of CH4 production rate (rCH4) were achieved at 0.5 mgcm−2 and −2 V vs. Ag/ AgCl (j= 7.5 mAcm−2). However, an interesting change in the reaction selectivity toward C2H4 was observed when reducing the particle size
from 60–80 to 40–60 and 25 nm. Interestingly, the results demonstrated that the use of smaller particles (25 nm) led to higher C2H4 production rates (rC2H4) and FE at 0.5 mgcm−2 and 7.5 mAcm−2, denoting the importance of particle size on the reaction selectivity.
In this study, we sought to address the use of Cu oxide dispersed on zinc oxide (ZnO) as electrocatalyst for the continuous gas-phase CO2 electroreduction to C2H4. The electroconversion of CO2 directly in gas phase allows avoiding the limitations of low solubility of CO2 in water that are present in common liquid-based systems [21–27], as well as the energy requirements for the separation of products [28]. Therefore, mass transfer constraints may be alleviated [29–36]. Besides, the literature demonstrated that the presence of Zn within the catalytic material may help to stabilize Cu+ atoms and remove impurities that can deactivate the electrocatalyst during CO2 electroconversion in the long run [37]. Furthermore, Keerthiga and Chetty [38] stated that this metal might suppress hydrogen formation, which is essential to increase the activity and selectivity for CO2 conversion.
Therefore, we propose here the deposition of the material onto a porous structure to form gas diffusion electrodes (GDEs) and membrane electrode assemblies (MEAs) to perform CO2 electroreduction tests in continuous mode using a divided filter-press type membrane reactor. Thus, the aim of the present study is the utilization of Cu oxide/ZnObased electrocatalysts for the continuous gas-phase electroconversion of CO2 into ethylene. Therefore, the following secondary objectives have been addressed to meet the target:
• synthesis of Cu oxide/ZnO particles and its deposition in GDEs and MEAs; • characterization of the prepared electrocatalysts and working electrodes.
The results are then compared with previous results obtained with pure Cu nanoparticles (particle size from 80 to 25 nm). This study provides new insights in the development of cheap, stable, durable and energy efficient electrocatalysts for an enhanced gas-phase CO2 electroreduction to C2 products, such as C2H4.

sections.heading: 2.1. Synthesis and characterization of Cu oxides/ZnO electrocatalysts
sections.text:
The preparation of the electrocatalytic material has been carried out at room temperature using a published synthesis procedure [39], adapted to incorporate the dispersion of the commercial ZnO particles (< 45 μm, 99.5% purity, ACROS organic). In brief, the particles are synthesized by reduction of CuCl2·2H2O (0.2M solution) with sodium borohydride (NaBH4) as reducing agent using a w/o microemulsion of water/polyethylenglycol-dodecylether (BRIJ® 30)/n-heptane. After complete reduction, a specific amount of ZnO is added to disperse the particles. The Cu oxides/ZnO particles weight ratio is 1:4. Subsequently, and after alternating magnetic stirring with ultrasounds for 1 h, acetone is added to the solution to break the microemulsion, causing phase separation. Afterwards, the precipitated obtained is filtered, washed several times with acetone and ultrapure water. Finally, the resulting precipitate is dried at 70 °C in a laboratory oven.
The prepared electrocatalytic materials have been characterized using different techniques. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images are collected using a JEOL JEM-2010 microscope, working at 200 kV. X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns are obtained with a Bruker D8 Advance diffractometer fitted with a copper tube. The optical setup included a Ni 0.5% CuKβ filter in the secondary beam so that only CuKα radiation illuminated the sample (CuKα1= 0.154059 nm and CuKα2= 0.154445 nm). The sample for XRD analysis is prepared after phase separation and washed with acetone. The samples are spread onto an Si wafer and measured in reflection geometry over the 20–90° 2θ range with a step of 0.10° and a counting time of 30 s per step. The
oxidation state of Cu on the catalyst surface is determined by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) measurements, performed with a VGMicrotech Multilab photoelectric spectrometer using a Mg Kα radiation source (1253.6 eV). During the analyses, a pressure of 5×10−10 mbar is used in the analysis chamber, while the patterns are obtained with a constant pass energy of 50 eV.

sections.heading: 2.2. Preparation and electrochemical characterization of the electrodes
sections.text:
The manufacturing process for the GDEs has been described elsewhere [36]. In short, a catalytic ink based on the synthesized particles, a Nafion solution and isopropanol is airbrushed onto a porous carbon paper (TGP-H-60, Toray Inc.). Cu oxides/ZnO-based GDEs are prepared with a geometric area (A) of 10 cm2 and a catalytic loading (L) of 0.5 mgcm−2, which is controlled by weighting. A Nafion 117 membrane is then assembled at 80 bar and 323 K to form a MEA.
The electrochemical behavior of the catalytic material is evaluated using cyclic voltammetry analyses in a standard three-electrode cell, in which a CO2-saturated 0.1M potassium bicarbonate (KHCO3) aqueous solution is used as electrolyte. Small portions of the GDEs are used as working electrodes, whereas a graphite rod and Ag/AgCl (sat. KCl) are used as the counter and the reference electrode, respectively. A MSTAT4 system (Arbin Instruments) is used to control the applied potential, which ranges from 0 V to −2 V vs. Ag/AgCl. The resulting current in each case is then normalized to the geometric area of the GDE pieces.

sections.heading: 2.3. Filter-press electrochemical cell and experimental conditions
sections.text:
The core of the experimental system for the continuous gas-phase CO2 electroreduction to hydrocarbons is a divided filter-press type cell (Micro Flow Cell, ElectroCell A/S) based on a MEA configuration at the cathode, which serves as both separator of the cell compartments and working electrode. A platinized titanium electrode (DSA-O2) is used as the counter electrode and a leak-free Ag/AgCl (sat. KCl), is utilized as the reference electrode. Humidified CO2 (180 mlmin−1) and a 0.1 M KHCO3 aqueous solution are used as catholyte and anolyte, respectively. A complete saturation of the CO2 stream is assumed. The CO2 reduction experiments are conducted using an AutoLab PGSTAT 302 N potentiostat which operates at galvanostatic conditions (j= 7.5 mAcm−2). This current density level was found to be the most optimized condition in previous studies, where both the effect of the applied voltage [35] and the influence of the current density [36] were evaluated using nanoparticulated Cu-based GDEs. The gas-phase reduction products are analyzed in a gas microchromatograph (3000
Micro GC, Inficon) equipped with thermal conductivity detector (TCD). The outlet gas stream of the electrochemical cell is measured every 5min for 45min (experimental time). Three replicates are performed to obtain an averaged concentration for each product. In addition, the condensable liquid products obtained at the reactor outlet (in coalescing filters) are analyzed using a headspace gas chromatograph (GCMSQP2010 Ultra Shimadzu) equipped with a flame ionization detector (FID).
The performance of the process is evaluated by the production rate per unit of cathode area and time (r, μmolm−2s−1), the ratio between production rates, namely selectivity (S), and the Faradaic efficiency (FE), which represents the efficiency at which electrons are transferred to form each product, according to the following equation:
=FE z n F Q x(%) 100 (1)
where z represents the number of electrons exchanged to form the desired product, n corresponds to the number of moles produced, F is the Faraday constant (F= 96,485 Cmol−1) and Q represents the total charge (C) passed through the system.
Additionally, the results are analyzed in terms of energy efficiency (EE), which is defined as the total energy used toward the formation of a specific desired product, according to the following equation:
=EE E E x FE(%) T (2)
where ET represents the theoretical voltage required in the CO2 electroreduction into the product of interest, whereas E is the real applied potential in the process.

sections.heading: 3.1. Physico-chemical characterization of the material
sections.text:
Fig. 1 shows different TEM images for the synthesized Cu oxides/ ZnO particles. As can be observed, the presence of ZnO particles is accompanied by the presence of some Cu nanoparticles forming aggregates with a size of around 300 nm. This finding might indicate that the dispersion of Cu nanoparticles on the ZnO can be enhanced. It is worth noting that the particle size may strongly influence the selectivity of the CO2-to-hydrocarbons reaction as demonstrated in literature in both liquid [40] and gas phase [36].
To further characterize the material, XRD measurements are also conducted. Fig. 2a and b show the XRD diffractograms for both the ZnO substrate and the Cu oxides/ZnO particles, respectively. Fig. 2a displays the characteristic peaks associated to ZnO (JCPDS 36–1451). Fig. 2b
also reveals the presence of the ZnO together with some additional peaks which can be attributed to the presence of CuO (JCPDS 48–1548), which is the major Cu-based component, and Cu2O (JCPDS 75–1531).
Furthermore, a XPS study has been carried out to properly evaluate the Cu oxidation state at the surface layer. Fig. 3 shows the high resolution Cu 2p XPS spectra obtained for the Cu oxides/ZnO. The characteristic doublet peaks corresponding to Cu 2p1/2 and Cu 2p3/2 at about ∼954 eV and ∼933 eV, respectively, and their shake-up satellite structures, are clearly observed [41,42]. The analysis of the Cu 2p3/2 peaks shows contributions at 933.2 eV and 935.2 eV which are related to the presence of CuO and Cu(OH)2, respectively. Interestingly, these results suggest the absence of Cu(I), that is (Cu2O), in the surface layer.

sections.heading: 3.2. Electrochemical characterization of the electrodes
sections.text:
The electrochemical behavior of the synthesized electrocatalyst is
firstly studied with cyclic voltammetry. Fig. 4 reports the current-voltage profiles obtained for the Cu oxides/ZnO-based electrodes as a function of applied voltage. In particular, Fig. 4a displays the cyclic voltammetric responses after 5 scans in the presence or absence (i.e. N2saturated electrolyte) of CO2. Similar performances can be observed if we compare the voltammetric profiles between 0 V and –1.0 V vs. Ag/ AgCl, which might be related to redox reactions on the GDE surface as well as the HER. Nevertheless, moderate differences in terms of catalytic activity (i.e. current density observed at the same potential) can be noted at more negative potentials than −1.1 V (specially at −2 V), which might be mainly associated with the fact that the electroreduction of the CO2 molecule is taken place.
Moreover, Fig. 4b shows the cyclic voltammetry curves for 5 and 40 scans in a CO2-saturated solution. There are only slight differences between the electrochemical responses which may indicate the electrochemical stability of the Cu oxides/ZnO electrodes with time.
Fig. 5 shows the Tafel plot profiles for Cu oxides/ZnO in comparison with Cu nanoparticles with different particle sizes. According to the Tafel equation, lower values of the Tafel slope involves lower kinetic barriers in the activation step of CO2 molecule (i.e. the initial one electron transfer to CO2 for the formation of the CO2− intermediate).
The Tafel slope for the larger Cu nanoparticulated-based GDE (i.e. 60–80 nm) is 118.7 mVdec−1, which is in accordance with previous results at Cu-based surfaces (116 mVdec−1) [43]. The slopes can be related to the electrochemical activation of CO2, which seems to be the rate-determining step in CO2 conversion systems. The Tafel slope for the Cu 40–60 nm-based GDE is lower (106.3 mVdec−1) than those achieved at Cu 60–80 nm (118.7 mVdec−1), whereas the use of Cu oxide/ZnO-based electrodes involves a more significant reduction of the activation barrier (103.3 mVdec−1), which can be associated with the synergic effect between metals. Nevertheless, there is a particle size
level where the influence of particle size is superior to the effect of combining metals due to the low Tafel slope observed at Cu 25 nm (101.6 mVdec−1), which suggests a lower kinetic barrier for CO2 electroconversion.

sections.heading: 3.3. Gas-phase CO2 electroreduction experiments
sections.text:
Fig. 6 shows the time evolution of the potential (E) and the C2H4 reaction rate (rC2H4) in the continuous gas-phase CO2 electroconversion at the Cu oxides/ZnO-based electrodes when applying a constant current density of 7.5 mAcm−2 at ambient conditions. Apart from the production of C2H4, different products such as CH4, CO, H2 and condensable liquid products (i.e. methanol, ethanol and acetone) have also been detected, as previously found in our gas phase CO2 reduction tests [35,36], even though the FE to liquid products does not exceed 0.6%. These results are in agreement with previous works reported in literature where oxide-derived Cu surfaces are preferred [44,45].
Pseudo-stable values for both the required potential and the C2H4 reaction rate are achieved after 10min of operation, even though fluctuations can be observed, which may be associated with the fact that CO2 is directly provided as gas at the cathode side and the presence of bubbles owing to the formation of H2 as well as the formation of gaseous products from CO2 reduction. In any case, pseudo-stable C2H4 rates can be obtained during the experimental time. Similar trends have been also reached for the rest of products during CO2 reduction reaction.
Table 2 and Fig. 7 show the comparison between the performance (i.e. r, S, and FE) for the Cu oxides/ZnO catalyst and the results achieved when using Cu nanoparticles with different particle size (Cu NP=60–80 nm, 40–60 nm and 25 nm) [36] at the same operating conditions (e.g. catalytic loading of 0.5 mgcm−2, j= 7.5 mAcm−2) for
the continuous gas phase CO2 electroconversion. FE is calculated assuming that 8 and 12 electrons are required to electroreduce CO2 into CH4 and C2H4, respectively.
The utilization of Cu oxides/ZnO-based electrodes shows a remarkable enhancement in terms of C2H4 rate (rC2H4= 487.9 μmol m−2s−1), which is more than two-fold improvement in comparison with the rC2H4 achieved when using Cu nanoparticles of 40–60 nm (rC2H4= 216.7 μmolm−2s−1). Cu nanoparticles 60–80 nm were not able to electroreduce CO2 to C2H4 but the results with Cu 25 nm-based electrodes were clearly superior (rC2H4= 1148 μmol m−2s−1). This might suggest that the C2H4 production is enhanced when combining metals due to the synergic effect between Zn and Cu, that is, the CO* intermediate may be formed at Zn sites, from which is then transferred to neighboring Cu active sites, where further conversion toward ethylene is taken place. In particular, after dimerization of CO* intermediate at Cu sites, several protonation steps allow the transformation of the dimerized species (i.e. COCOH) into the target product [46]. However, reducing the particle size of the electrocatalyst at certain level seems to be the parameter defining process performance. Therefore, a fine control of the Cu/Zn aggregates size appears to be an essential issue that need to be tackled.
Furthermore, the Cu oxides/ZnO-based electrode displays a similar FE to C2H4 compared to the result reached at Cu 25 nm NP (91.1% vs. 92.8%). Interestingly, these FE values are sufficiently high to be considered commercially applicable.
Moreover, SC2H4/CH4 and SC2H4/H2 reached a value of 139 and 2, respectively, when Cu oxides/ZnO-based GDEs are used as working electrodes, whereas lower values are achieved (51.2 and 0.99, respectively) for the Cu 40–60 nm catalysts. Besides, SC2H4/CH4 and SC2H4/H2 are 30.5 and 3.1, respectively, when Cu nanoparticles of 25 nm are used, which may denote the key effect of combining materials on the selectivity of the CO2 reduction reaction toward C2H4, even though SC2H4/H2 is slightly improved at Cu 25 nm NP.
These findings may be attributed to an improvement in the adsorption of reaction intermediates such as CO* onto the catalytic surface that favors the electroreduction of CO2 into C2H4 over CH4 formation, as discussed by Chang et al., where a better selectivity for the formation of C2H4 was associated with an improvement in the adsorption of the *CO intermediate onto the Cu surface when using bimetallic Cu-based core-shell nanoparticles for CO2 conversion [18]. Besides, other authors suggest that the structure of the multimetallic electrocatalyst may influence the selectivity toward C2 products such as C2H4, since the adsorbed CO intermediate might be dimerized to the intermediate COCOH that is finally converted to C2-based products [19].
Moreover, the utilization of the Cu oxide/ZnO-based electrocatalytic material does not involve higher energy consumption in comparison to that required for Cu 40–60 nm electrocatalyst for C2H4 production. However, the lowest potential required is reached at Cu NP of 25 nm-based working electrodes (i.e. −1.7 V vs. Ag/AgCl), denoting the importance of developing electrocatalysts with controlled particle size and geometry to make this process closer to practical applications from an energy viewpoint.
Therefore, the coupling between Cu and a secondary metal seems to be one of the key aspect to reduce the reaction energy barrier during the CO2 electroconversion (i.e. CO*) to C2H4 over CH4, even though electrocatalyst size also plays an important role. Besides, another issue that might have a significant influence on reaction selectivity is the O and H affinities of the secondary metal in combined electrocatalytic materials. Therefore, the choice of the secondary metal is crucial owing to its important role altering inherent adsorption energetics [47], which affects reaction pathways.
Finally, Table 3 and Fig. 8 present a comparison between the findings of the present study and the results reported in literature for the production of C2H4 from CO2 electroreduction at different Cu-based electrocatalysts [6,9–12,14,15,18–27,29–32,36,40,48–81], including
the production rate, rC2H4 (Table 3), FE and EE (Fig. 8). It is important to take into consideration that different operating conditions and cell configurations are applied in each study.
As observed, the performance of the prepared Cu oxides/ZnO-based electrodes is clearly superior to the main production rates reported for the electroreduction of CO2 to C2H4 (r= 488 μmol m−2s−1). Nevertheless, r is still far from the value achieved when using Cu nanoparticles of 25 nm (r= 1148 μmolm−2s−1), which again denotes the importance of the electrocatalyst size in the production of C2H4 [36]. Therefore, the control of the Cu aggregates of the prepared multimetallic electrocatalyst appears to be essential to achieve an enhanced

Fig. 8a shows that the FE to C2H4 reported in the present manuscript (91.1%) at E= −2.5 V is among the highest FE values reported so far. Moreover, Fig. 8b. indicates that the lower the applied voltage, the higher the EE. A maximum EE of 20% is achieved using the so prepared Cu oxide/ZnO-based electrodes. In any case, the values presented still need to be improved to make this technology closer to industrial applications, where stability, the required active surface area and the catalytic material cost are crucial parameters that must be considered in the short term.

sections.heading: 4. Conclusions
sections.text:
In this study, the continuous gas-phase carbon dioxide electroreduction to ethylene was investigated at room temperature in a filterpress type electrochemical cell at Cu oxides/ZnO-based surfaces. The working electrodes were prepared by airbrushing the Cu oxides/ZnO particles at catalytic loadings of 0.5 mgcm−2, followed by the coupling of a cationic exchange membrane to form membrane electrode assemblies. The physico-chemical characterization results of the electrocatalytic material via transmission electron microscopy, X-ray diffraction and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy revealed that the catalyst is composed of large aggregates (around 300 nm) based on Cu oxides (CuO and Cu2O) supported on a commercial ZnO substrate. The electrochemical activity of the material was evaluated by cyclic voltammetry test and Tafel plot analyses.
The experiments in cell showed an ethylene production rate of 487.9 μmolm−2s−1 with a Faradaic efficiency of 91.1%. These results are significantly superior to most of the previous results for ethylene production at Cu-based surfaces, which revealed the advantages of combining Cu with Zn, but lower than those results at 25 nm Cu nanoparticles, which denotes the importance of controlling the size of the Cu-based aggregates. Furthermore, the production rate ratio between ethylene and methane was almost three-fold improved (SC2H4/ CH4= 139) in comparison with the use of pure Cu nanoparticles with different particle sizes.
Overall, the application of Cu oxides/ZnO electrocatalysts is beneficial for an enhanced ethylene formation from carbon dioxide conversion owing to its ability to both lead the reaction to more reduces species and reduce the effect of the hydrogen gas evolution reaction, even though the performance of the process still needs to be improved to make the technology feasible in the future.
